anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: List the red flags for back pain.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Cauda equina (saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel, bilateral sciatica), malignancy (age >50, weight loss, night pain, past cancer), infection (fever, IVDU, immunosuppression), fracture (trauma, osteoporosis, steroids), and inflammatory (young, morning stiffness >30 min, better with exercise).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: In which direction does a disc usually herniate, and why?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Posterolaterally — the posterior longitudinal ligament reinforces the disc centrally, so the weak point is posterolateral (where it compresses the nerve root).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Which nerve root does an L4/L5 disc prolapse typically compress, and what is the deficit?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: The L5 root (the traversing root) → weak big-toe/great-toe extension (EHL), numb dorsum of foot, difficulty heel-walking.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Which nerve root does an L5/S1 disc prolapse typically compress, and what is the deficit?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: The S1 root → weak plantarflexion, numb sole/lateral foot, and a reduced ankle jerk.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Why does a paracentral disc hit the LOWER (traversing) nerve root rather than the exiting one?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: The exiting root has already left above the disc; the traversing root (destined to exit at the level below) crosses the posterolateral disc and is compressed — so an L4/5 disc affects L5.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is sciatica, and which test reproduces it?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Radicular leg pain in a dermatomal (L5/S1) distribution; the straight-leg-raise (Lasègue’s) test reproduces it by stretching the sciatic nerve.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: At what level does the spinal cord end, and what lies below it?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: At L1/L2 (the conus medullaris); below it the cauda equina (the lumbosacral nerve roots) floats in CSF.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What are the red-flag features of cauda equina syndrome?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Saddle anaesthesia, painless urinary retention (then overflow incontinence), faecal incontinence / loss of anal tone, and bilateral sciatica & leg weakness.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: How is suspected cauda equina syndrome managed?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: It is a surgical emergency — urgent MRI and decompression; delay risks permanent bladder, bowel & sexual dysfunction.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Contrast the motor signs of a cord (UMN) lesion with a cauda equina (LMN) lesion.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: A cord lesion → UMN signs below the level (spastic, hyperreflexic, up-going plantars, a sensory level); cauda equina → LMN signs (flaccid, areflexic, down-going plantars, saddle/root sensory loss).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What are the features of malignant spinal cord compression?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Back pain, a sensory level, UMN signs below and bladder involvement → urgent MRI whole spine and steroids (a metastatic emergency).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Describe an osteoporotic wedge (compression) fracture.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Loss of anterior vertebral height from axial/flexion load in weakened bone (elderly, steroids); usually stable and treated conservatively.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is a burst fracture, and why can it be dangerous?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: An axial-loading fracture with retropulsion of bone into the spinal canal — potentially unstable, risking cord/cauda injury.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is a Chance fracture?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: A flexion-distraction (“seat-belt”) fracture through the vertebral body & posterior elements; often associated with intra-abdominal injuries.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Define kyphosis, lordosis and scoliosis.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Kyphosis — excessive thoracic flexion curve; lordosis — excessive lumbar extension curve; scoliosis — lateral curvature with vertebral rotation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is spondylolisthesis?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Forward slippage of one vertebra on the one below (commonly L5 on S1) — may cause back pain & radiculopathy.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is spinal stenosis, and its classic symptom?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Narrowing of the spinal canal (degenerative/spondylotic) → neurogenic claudication (leg pain on walking, relieved by flexion/sitting).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: At what vertebral level is a lumbar puncture performed, and why there?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: At L3/L4 or L4/L5 — below the conus (L1/2), so the needle meets only mobile cauda equina roots rather than the cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is Tuffier's line?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: A line joining the iliac crests, crossing the L4 spinous process (≈ the L4/5 interspace) — the landmark for a lumbar puncture.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: List, in order, the layers pierced during a lumbar puncture to reach CSF.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Skin → superficial fascia → supraspinous ligament → interspinous ligament → ligamentum flavum → epidural space → dura → arachnoid → subarachnoid space (CSF).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What is the difference between spinal and epidural anaesthesia?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Spinal injects into the subarachnoid space (CSF) (dural puncture); epidural injects into the epidural (extradural) space (no dural puncture).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Distinguish spina bifida occulta, meningocele and myelomeningocele.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Occulta — failed vertebral arch fusion only (hair tuft/dimple, usually asymptomatic); meningocele — meninges herniate (cord normal); myelomeningocele — meninges and neural tissue herniate → deficit (± Chiari II & hydrocephalus).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: How are neural tube defects prevented and screened for?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Prevented by peri-conceptional folic acid; screened by a raised maternal serum AFP (and ultrasound).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What does the straight-leg-raise test assess, and the femoral stretch test?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: SLR stretches the sciatic nerve → L5/S1 radiculopathy; the femoral stretch (prone knee flexion) targets the L2–L4 roots (anterior thigh pain).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Give the root values of the knee and ankle jerks.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: Knee jerk = L3/L4; ankle jerk = S1.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: Give dermatome anchors for T4, T10, L1, L5 and S1.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: T4 nipple · T10 umbilicus · L1 groin · L5 big toe/dorsum of foot · S1 little toe/sole.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What does an up-going plantar response indicate?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: An upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion (Babinski sign) — pointing to a cord/brain lesion rather than a root/cauda problem.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What suggests inflammatory (rather than mechanical) back pain?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: A young patient with insidious pain, morning stiffness >30 min, pain that is better with exercise & worse with rest, and night pain (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.front: What three columns determine spinal stability (Denis)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.back: The anterior, middle & posterior columns; involvement of ≥2 columns suggests instability.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: How many vertebrae are there, and in what regional distribution?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: 33: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral & 4 fused coccygeal (24 mobile presacral).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Which spinal curvatures are primary, and which secondary?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Primary (kyphotic) — thoracic & sacral (present at birth); secondary (lordotic) — cervical & lumbar (develop after birth with head control & walking).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What are the components of a typical vertebra?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A body (weight-bearing) and a vertebral arch (pedicles + laminae) enclosing the vertebral foramen, with one spinous, two transverse and paired superior/inferior articular processes.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is transmitted by the intervertebral foramen?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The spinal nerve (with its dorsal root ganglion) and accompanying radicular vessels; it is narrowed by disc prolapse or osteophytes → radiculopathy.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What feature is unique to cervical vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The foramen transversarium in each transverse process — transmitting the vertebral artery (C1–C6); cervical vertebrae also have bifid spinous processes (C3–6).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What distinguishes thoracic vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A heart-shaped body with costal facets/demifacets (for rib heads) and transverse costal facets (for rib tubercles), plus a long, downward-pointing spinous process.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What distinguishes lumbar vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A large, kidney-shaped body, no costal facets or transverse foramina, a short blunt (“hatchet”) spinous process and a mamillary process.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Describe the atlas (C1).
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: It has no body and no spinous process — just anterior & posterior arches and lateral masses; its superior facets articulate with the occipital condyles.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Describe the axis (C2).
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: It bears the dens (odontoid process), which projects up as a pivot for the atlas to rotate around.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is the vertebra prominens?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: C7 — it has a long, non-bifid spinous process that is a palpable surface landmark.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Name the key features of the sacrum.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: 5 fused vertebrae; the sacral promontory, ala, anterior & posterior sacral foramina, median crest, and the sacral hiatus (for caudal anaesthesia).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Classify the intervertebral joints, and describe the disc.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Secondary cartilaginous (symphyses); the intervertebral disc = an outer annulus fibrosus and inner nucleus pulposus (a shock absorber).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What are the uncovertebral joints (of Luschka)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Small clefts on the lateral margins of the cervical vertebral bodies; they can develop osteophytes that narrow the intervertebral foramen.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Classify the zygapophyseal (facet) joints.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Synovial plane joints between the superior & inferior articular processes of adjacent vertebrae.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: How does facet orientation determine regional movement?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Cervical — oblique (all movements); thoracic — coronal (rotation, limited by ribs); lumbar — sagittal (flexion/extension, little rotation).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What movement occurs at the atlanto-occipital joint?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Flexion & extension — nodding the head (“YES”).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What movement occurs at the atlanto-axial joint?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Rotation around the dens — shaking the head (“NO”); it provides ~50% of neck rotation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What does the transverse ligament of the atlas do?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: It holds the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas (part of the cruciate ligament), preventing posterior displacement of the dens onto the cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Name the other craniovertebral ligaments.
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The alar ligaments (dens → occipital condyles, limit rotation), the apical ligament, and the tectorial membrane (upward continuation of the PLL).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Why is transverse ligament rupture or a dens fracture dangerous?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: It causes atlanto-axial instability — the dens can compress the spinal cord (potentially fatal); a recognised risk in rheumatoid arthritis and trauma.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What does the anterior longitudinal ligament do?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Runs down the front of the vertebral bodies and is the only spinal ligament to limit extension (it is broad & strong).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What does the posterior longitudinal ligament do?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Runs down the back of the bodies (within the canal); it limits flexion and, being narrow centrally, directs disc herniation posterolaterally.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is the ligamentum flavum?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: An elastic ligament connecting adjacent laminae; it resists flexion and is the last ligament pierced (before the dura) in a lumbar puncture.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is the ligamentum nuchae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The fibroelastic cervical continuation of the supraspinous & interspinous ligaments — a median septum providing muscle attachment and helping support the head.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is a Jefferson fracture?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A burst fracture of the atlas (C1) ring from axial loading (e.g. diving into shallow water).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is a hangman's fracture?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: A bilateral fracture through the pars interarticularis/pedicles of C2 (axis) from hyperextension.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What is a cervical rib, and its clinical consequence?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: An extra rib arising from C7; it can compress the brachial plexus/subclavian vessels → thoracic outlet syndrome.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: What are sacralisation and lumbarisation?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: Transitional vertebral anomalies at the L5/S1 junction — sacralisation (L5 fuses to the sacrum) or lumbarisation (S1 becomes a separate lumbar-like vertebra).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.front: Which regions of the spine are most mobile, and which is splinted?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.back: The cervical & lumbar regions are the most mobile; the thoracic spine is splinted by the ribs.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A large central lumbar disc prolapse causing saddle anaesthesia, painless urinary retention and bilateral sciatica indicates:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: This triad (saddle anaesthesia, bladder dysfunction, bilateral sciatica) is cauda equina syndrome — a surgical emergency requiring urgent MRI and decompression.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: An L4/L5 disc prolapse most commonly compresses which nerve root?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: A paracentral L4/5 disc compresses the traversing L5 root (the exiting L4 root has already left above the disc).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Weak plantarflexion and a reduced ankle jerk suggest compression of which root (and which disc)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The S1 root (typically an L5/S1 disc) supplies plantarflexion and the ankle jerk; its compression weakens plantarflexion and reduces the ankle reflex.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Intervertebral discs most commonly herniate in which direction?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Discs herniate posterolaterally because the posterior longitudinal ligament reinforces the midline; this is where the traversing nerve root is compressed.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: The spinal cord (conus medullaris) usually ends at which vertebral level in adults?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The adult spinal cord ends at L1/L2 as the conus medullaris; below this the cauda equina roots descend within the subarachnoid space.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A lumbar puncture is performed at L3/4 or L4/5 primarily because:
options: It is below the conus medullaris, so the needle avoids the cord
There is no CSF higher up
The ligamentum flavum is absent there
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: LP is done below the conus (L1/2) so the needle enters CSF among the mobile cauda equina roots rather than risking the spinal cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Tuffier's line, joining the iliac crests, crosses which spinous process?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Tuffier's (the intercristal) line crosses the L4 spinous process (≈ the L4/5 interspace), the landmark for lumbar puncture.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: During a midline lumbar puncture, which ligament is pierced immediately before the dura?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The order is supraspinous → interspinous → ligamentum flavum → epidural space → dura; the ligamentum flavum is the last ligament before the epidural space and dura.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia differs from epidural anaesthesia in that spinal anaesthesia:
options: Is injected into the CSF (subarachnoid space)
Uses a larger volume of anaesthetic
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Spinal anaesthesia is injected through the dura into the CSF (subarachnoid space); epidural anaesthesia is placed in the epidural space without dural puncture.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A cord (upper motor neuron) lesion is distinguished from a cauda equina (lower motor neuron) lesion by:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: A cord lesion produces UMN signs below the level (spasticity, hyperreflexia, up-going plantars, a sensory level); cauda equina produces LMN signs (flaccid, areflexic).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Which feature is a 'red flag' pointing to malignancy as a cause of back pain?
options: Age >50 with weight loss and night pain
Improvement with exercise in a young patient
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Age >50, weight loss, unremitting night pain and a history of cancer are red flags for malignant (often metastatic) back pain.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Malignant spinal cord compression is suggested by back pain plus:
options: A sensory level with UMN signs below and bladder involvement
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Cord compression gives a sensory level and UMN signs below the lesion with sphincter involvement — an oncological emergency requiring urgent MRI and steroids.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: An osteoporotic vertebral fracture is typically which type?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Osteoporotic fractures are typically anterior wedge (compression) fractures with loss of anterior vertebral height.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A flexion-distraction 'seat-belt' vertebral fracture is called a:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: A Chance fracture is a horizontal flexion-distraction injury through the vertebra, classically from a lap seat-belt and often associated with intra-abdominal injury.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: Neurogenic claudication (leg pain on walking, relieved by sitting/flexion) is characteristic of:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Lumbar spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication — leg pain/heaviness on walking relieved by flexing forward (which widens the canal).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: A myelomeningocele differs from a meningocele in that a myelomeningocele:
options: Contains herniated neural tissue as well as meninges
Is the same as spina bifida occulta
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: A myelomeningocele herniates both meninges and neural tissue, causing neurological deficit (and often Chiari II/hydrocephalus); a meningocele contains meninges only.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: The ankle jerk reflex tests which nerve root?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The ankle jerk is an S1 reflex; the knee jerk is L3/L4.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: The straight-leg-raise (Lasègue's) test primarily assesses which nerve roots?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: SLR stretches the sciatic nerve and reproduces pain from L5/S1 root irritation; the femoral stretch test assesses the higher L2–L4 roots.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.question: The umbilicus corresponds to which dermatome, a useful marker of a sensory level?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The umbilicus is the T10 dermatome (nipple T4, groin L1) — helpful for identifying a sensory level in cord lesions.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: How many vertebrae are there in total (including fused sacral and coccygeal)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: There are 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 fused coccygeal (24 are mobile presacral).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Which curvatures are the PRIMARY (present at birth) curvatures?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The thoracic and sacral (kyphotic) curvatures are primary; the cervical and lumbar (lordotic) curvatures are secondary, developing with head control and walking.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The foramen transversarium, transmitting the vertebral artery, is characteristic of which vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The foramen transversarium is unique to cervical vertebrae and transmits the vertebral artery (through C1–C6).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Costal facets (demifacets) on the vertebral body are found on which vertebrae?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets/demifacets on their bodies (for rib heads) and transverse costal facets (for rib tubercles).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Which structure is ABSENT in the atlas (C1)?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The atlas has no body and no spinous process — it is a ring of anterior and posterior arches with lateral masses.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The dens (odontoid process) is a feature of which vertebra?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The dens projects upward from the body of the axis (C2) and serves as the pivot for the atlas.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The intervertebral disc joint is classified as a:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: Intervertebral (body-to-body) joints are secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses); the disc has an outer annulus fibrosus and inner nucleus pulposus.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The zygapophyseal (facet) joints are:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: Facet joints between the articular processes are synovial plane joints; their orientation determines the movement permitted in each region.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Nodding the head 'yes' (flexion/extension) occurs mainly at which joint?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The atlanto-occipital joint (C0–C1) permits flexion/extension — the 'yes' nod; the atlanto-axial joint permits rotation ('no').

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Rotation of the head ('no') occurs at the atlanto-axial joint, pivoting around the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The atlanto-axial joint is a pivot: the atlas (and skull) rotate around the dens of the axis, providing about half of neck rotation.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The transverse ligament of the atlas functions to:
options: Hold the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas
Support the head like a strut
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The transverse ligament holds the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas; its rupture (e.g. in rheumatoid arthritis) allows the dens to compress the cord.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Which spinal ligament is the only one that limits EXTENSION?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The anterior longitudinal ligament, running along the front of the vertebral bodies, is the only spinal ligament that limits extension.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The narrow posterior longitudinal ligament contributes to disc herniation being directed:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: Because the PLL reinforces the midline posteriorly, discs herniate posterolaterally, where they compress the traversing nerve root.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: The elastic ligament connecting adjacent laminae, pierced last before the dura in a lumbar puncture, is the:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The ligamentum flavum (elastic, between laminae) resists flexion and is the last ligament traversed before the epidural space and dura in an LP.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: A burst fracture of the C1 (atlas) ring from axial loading is a:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: A Jefferson fracture is a burst fracture of the atlas ring caused by axial loading (e.g. diving into shallow water).

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: A bilateral fracture of the C2 pars interarticularis from hyperextension is called a:
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: A hangman's fracture is a bilateral fracture through the pars interarticularis/pedicles of the axis (C2) from hyperextension.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: A cervical rib arises from which vertebra and can cause which syndrome?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: A cervical rib arises from C7 and can compress the lower brachial plexus/subclavian vessels, causing thoracic outlet syndrome.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Thoracic spine movement is most restricted because it is:
options: Splinted by the ribs and has coronally-oriented facets
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: The thoracic spine is splinted by the rib cage and its coronally-oriented facets favour rotation but limit overall mobility, making it the least mobile region.

anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.question: Which vertebra is the 'vertebra prominens' with a long, non-bifid spinous process used as a surface landmark?
anatomy__BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joint.explanation: C7 is the vertebra prominens; its long, non-bifid spinous process is easily palpated at the base of the neck.
